p.src: The Pilgrim took leave of the Bodhisattva, lowered his cloud, hung the cassock on a fragrant nanmu tree, drew out his staff, and fought his way into Black Wind Cave, where not a single lesser demon was to be found. It turned out that when they saw the Bodhisattva appear and subdue the old monster, making him roll upon the ground, they had all fled in haste. The Pilgrim gave full rein to his fury. He piled dry firewood against every one of the cave's several gates and set it alight both front and rear, turning Black Wind Cave into a Red Wind Cave. Then he took the cassock, mounted an auspicious radiance, and headed straight back north.

p.src: Now Tripitaka, seeing that the Pilgrim had still not returned, grew deeply uneasy. He could not tell whether the Bodhisattva had refused to come or whether the Pilgrim had made an excuse and run away. While his mind was churning with wild conjectures, he suddenly saw brilliant many-colored mist in midair. The Pilgrim dropped before the steps, knelt, and said, “Master, I have brought the cassock back.” Tripitaka was overjoyed. All the monks rejoiced as well, saying, “Wonderful, wonderful! Only today have our lives finally been spared.” Taking the cassock, Tripitaka said, “Wukong, when you left this morning, you promised to return by noon, after the meal. Why have you not come back until now, when the sun is already in the west?” The Pilgrim then gave a full account of how he had invited the Bodhisattva to work a transformation and subdue the monster. When Tripitaka had heard him out, he set up an incense altar and bowed in worship toward the south. Then he said, “Disciple, now that we have the Buddha's robe back, let us quickly gather and pack our belongings and depart.” The Pilgrim said, “There is no hurry, no hurry. It is almost nightfall, and this is no time to travel. Let us wait and set out early tomorrow.” The monks all knelt together and said, “Lord Sun is right. For one thing, it is late; for another, we have vows to fulfill. Now that all is fortunately well and the treasure has been recovered, please allow us to redeem our vows and invite you, my lord, to partake of the blessed feast. Tomorrow morning we shall see you off on your westward journey.” The Pilgrim said, “Quite right, quite right.” Just look at those monks: they emptied their purses and brought out all the property they had rescued from the fire. Each contributed whatever he possessed, and together they prepared vegetarian offerings, burned votive paper in thanks for peace and safety, and recited several scriptures for averting calamity and dispelling misfortune. The rites were completed that evening.

p.src: When he had finished looking, the Pilgrim said, “Please go on, Master. It is surely a decent village, and just the place to seek lodging.” The elder urged the white horse onward and soon reached the entrance to the village street. There they saw a young man coming hurriedly out of the street with a bold and vigorous air. A cotton cloth was wrapped around his head, and he wore a blue padded jacket. He carried an umbrella and a pack, had his loincloth gathered and his trousers bound tight, and wore a pair of three-eared straw sandals. The Pilgrim casually reached out and seized him, saying, “Where are you going? Let me ask you something: what place is this?” The man struggled desperately and shouted, “Am I the only man in the whole village, that you must pick me to question?” The Pilgrim smiled placatingly and said, “Do not be angry, benefactor. ‘Make things convenient for others, and you make things convenient for yourself.’ What harm can it do you simply to tell me the name of this place? Perhaps I can relieve you of your troubles as well.” Unable to wrench himself free, the man jumped about in fury and cried, “What rotten luck! What rotten luck! As if the master's abuse at home were not enough, now I have run into this baldhead and must endure his pestering too.” The Pilgrim said, “If you have the strength, pry open my hand, and you may go.” The man twisted left and right, but could not budge him; it was as though he were clamped in a pair of iron pincers. Furious, he dropped his pack, flung aside his umbrella, and clawed at the Pilgrim with both hands as thick and fast as raindrops. The Pilgrim steadied the luggage with one hand and held the man at bay with the other. No matter how the fellow flailed and struggled, he could not lay a finger on him. The more the Pilgrim refused to let go, the more frantic the man became, raging like thunder. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, is that not someone else coming over there? You can simply ask that person instead. Why keep holding on to this man? Let him go.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “You do not understand, Master. There would be no fun in asking anyone else. It has to be this fellow if we are to learn something worthwhile.” The man, still held fast by the Pilgrim, had no choice but to say, “This place lies within the borders of the Kingdom of Ü-Tsang and is called Gao Village. More than half the households in the village bear the surname Gao, and that is why it is called Gao Village. Now let me go.” The Pilgrim continued, “Judging by your traveling gear, you are not merely going somewhere nearby. Tell me truthfully where you are going and exactly what business takes you there. Only then shall I release you.”

p.src: Having no choice, the man told him the truth: “I am a servant of Old Master Gao, and my name is Gao Cai. My master has a youngest daughter who is just twenty years old and has never been betrothed. Three years ago, a demon took possession of her, and for these three years the creature has made himself the family’s son-in-law. My master was displeased and said, ‘Having a demon for a daughter’s husband cannot be allowed to continue: first, it disgraces the family; second, it leaves us with no respectable in-laws to associate with.’ He has long wanted to be rid of the demon. But the demon would not leave. Instead, he shut the daughter in the rear quarters, and for nearly half a year now has not let her come out to see anyone in the family. My master gave me several taels of silver and ordered me to seek out an exorcist who could capture the monster. I have scarcely rested all this time. Altogether I have brought back three or four men, but they were all useless monks and spineless Daoists, none of whom could subdue the demon. Just now my master gave me a sound scolding, saying I was incapable of getting anything done. Then he gave me another five mace of silver for travelling expenses and told me to find a skilled exorcist to subdue it. Who would have thought I should run into a baleful brute like you, who seized hold of me and delayed my journey? Thus I have been vexed both at home and abroad, and in my helplessness I shouted at you. I never expected you to have such a grip. Since I could not wrench myself free, I had no choice but to tell you the truth. Now please let me go.” The Pilgrim said, “This is your good fortune. I have found work to do; the business fits us together perfectly. You need not travel any farther, nor need you spend that silver. We are not useless monks or spineless Daoists. We truly have some ability and are well practised in capturing demons. As the saying goes, ‘One visit calls upon the physician, and at the same time cures the eye.’ Please go back and report to your master that we are the imperial brother and holy monk sent from the court of the Eastern Land, journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures, and that we are highly skilled at subduing demons and binding monsters.” Gao Cai said, “You must not lead me astray. I am already full of anger. If you deceive me and turn out to have no real ability, and cannot capture the demon, will you not bring trouble upon me and make me suffer another scolding?” The Pilgrim said, “I guarantee I shall not let you down. Lead me to the gate of your master’s house.” The man had no other recourse, so he picked up his bundle and umbrella, turned back, and led master and disciple to the gate. “Reverend sirs,” he said, “please sit for a moment on the mounting-block while I go inside and inform my master.” Only then did the Pilgrim release him. They set down the luggage and took charge of the horse, while master and disciple waited beside the gate, one sitting and the other standing.

p.src: Gao Cai entered the main gate and went straight towards the central hall, where he happened to run into Old Master Gao. The old master cursed him: “You thick-skinned beast! Why have you come back instead of going to find someone?” Gao Cai put down his bundle and umbrella and said, “I beg to report to my master: just as I left the end of the street, I suddenly met two monks, one riding a horse and the other carrying luggage on a shoulder pole. The latter seized me and would not let go, demanding to know where I was going. Again and again I refused to tell him, but he pestered me until I had no choice. Unable to get free, I told him every detail of my master’s affair. He was delighted and said he wanted to capture that monster for us.” Old Gao asked, “Where have they come from?” Gao Cai replied, “They say they are the imperial brother and holy monk sent from the court of the Eastern Land, travelling to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures.” The old master said, “Since they are monks who have come from afar, they may indeed possess some real ability. Where are they now?” Gao Cai said, “They are waiting outside the gate.”

p.src: The old master hurriedly changed his clothes and came out with Gao Cai to welcome them, calling, “Reverend sir!” Sanzang heard him and quickly turned around; the old man had already reached him. The old man wore a cap of black damask, a pale green robe of Sichuan brocade, calfskin boots the colour of unpolished rice, and a dark green sash. Coming forward with a smiling greeting, he said, “Reverend sirs, allow me to salute you.” Sanzang returned the salute, but the Pilgrim stood without moving. Seeing how fierce and ugly he looked, the old man dared not salute him. The Pilgrim said, “Why do you not bow to old Sun?” The old man was rather frightened and cried to Gao Cai, “You wretched boy, are you trying to get me killed? We already have one hideous, monstrous son-in-law at home whom we cannot get rid of. Why have you brought this Thunder Duke here to torment me as well?” The Pilgrim said, “Old Gao, you have lived to such a great age, yet you still understand nothing. If you judge people solely by their looks, you are altogether mistaken. Old Sun may be ugly, but I possess some ability. If I capture the demon and seize the fiend for your household, take your son-in-law prisoner, and restore your daughter to you, that will surely be a good deed. Why keep harping on my appearance?” Hearing this, the old master trembled with fear. He had no choice but to summon his courage and say, “Please come inside.” Once invited, the Pilgrim led the white horse, told Gao Cai to carry the luggage, and went inside with Sanzang. Without asking whether it was proper, he tied the horse to a pillar in the open hall, pulled over a polished lacquer armchair, and asked his master to sit down. Then he pulled over another chair and sat down beside him. Old Gao said, “This young reverend certainly makes himself at home.” The Pilgrim replied, “If you were willing to let me stay for half a year, I would make myself still more at home.”

p.src: Once they were seated, Old Gao asked, “My young servant said just now that you two reverend monks came from the Eastern Land?” Tripitaka replied, “Indeed we are. This poor monk is journeying to the Western Heaven by imperial command to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. As we happened to pass your honored estate, we came only to request lodging for one night and will depart early tomorrow.” Old Gao said, “If you two merely came for lodging, why did you say you could catch monsters?” Pilgrim said, “Since we are asking for lodging, I thought I might catch a few monsters in passing for sport. May I ask how many monsters there are in your household?” Old Gao cried, “Heavens! How could we bear to have any more? This one monstrous son-in-law has already tormented us out of our wits.” Pilgrim said, “Tell me his whole history and how great his powers are, from beginning to end, so that I may catch him for you.” Old Gao said, “From ancient times until the present, no ghosts, goblins, evil spirits, or demons have ever been known to cause trouble in our village. But I had the misfortune to have no sons and only three daughters: the eldest is called Xianglan, the second Yulan, and the third Cuilan. The elder two were betrothed from childhood to families of this village. Only for the youngest did I intend to take in a husband, hoping he would live with me as a resident son-in-law in my old age, uphold the household, and attend to its work and duties. Unexpectedly, three years ago a man appeared who was quite presentable in looks. He said that he came from Mount Fuling, that his surname was Zhu, and that having neither parents above nor brothers below, he wished to become a resident son-in-law. Seeing that he was a man without roots or entanglements, I took him in as my son-in-law. When he first entered the household, he was diligent enough: he plowed and harrowed the fields without ox or implements; and harvested the crops without blade or tool; he went out at dusk and returned at dawn, and truly did well. There was only one thing: his face had a way of changing.” Pilgrim asked, “How did it change?” Old Gao said, “When he first came, he was a stout, dark-skinned fellow. Later he turned into a fool with a long snout and great ears, a row of bristles down the back of his head, and a coarse, frightening body; his head and face looked just like a pig’s. His appetite is enormous too: at one meal he eats three to five dou of rice, and even for his morning snack it takes a hundred or so griddle cakes to fill him. Fortunately, he eats only vegetarian fare; if he ate meat and drank wine as well, all my property and farmland would be consumed without a trace in less than half a year.” Tripitaka said, “He eats so much only because he works so much.” Old Gao said, “His eating is a small matter. Now he can also raise winds; he comes in clouds and departs in mist, sending stones rolling and sand flying. He has frightened my entire household and all our neighbors so badly that none of us can live in peace. He has also shut my young daughter Cuilan in the rear quarters. For fully half a year we have not seen her and do not even know whether she is alive or dead. Thus we know he is a monster, and we want to invite an exorcist to drive him away.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “What difficulty is there in that? Set your mind at ease, old man. Tonight I am certain to catch him for you, make him write a document dissolving the marriage, and return your daughter to you. How would that be?” Old Gao rejoiced greatly and said, “Taking him in as a son-in-law was bad enough, but he has also ruined my good name and estranged so many of my relatives. If you can only catch him, what need is there for any document? Please uproot the evil for me once and for all.” Pilgrim said, “Easy, easy. When night falls, you shall see how it turns out.”

Old Gao rejoiced greatly and said, “Taking him in as a son-in-law was bad enough, but he has also ruined my good name and estranged so many of my relatives.
If you can only catch him, what need is there for any document?
Please uproot the evil for me once and for all.”
Pilgrim said, “Easy, easy.
When night falls, you shall see how it turns out.”

p.src: The old man was overjoyed and only then ordered the tables and chairs to be wiped and arranged and a vegetarian meal to be set out. When the meal was finished, evening was approaching, and the old man asked, “What weapons will you need? How many men should accompany you? We should prepare them while there is still time.” Pilgrim said, “I have my own weapon.” The old man said, “You two have only that priest’s staff. How could such a staff defeat the fiend?” Pilgrim immediately took an embroidery needle from his ear, held it between his fingers, and waved it once into the wind. It became an iron staff with golden bands as thick as a rice bowl. Holding it before Old Gao, he said, “Look at this staff. How does it compare with the weapons in your household? Will it serve to beat that monster?” Old Gao asked again, “Since you have a weapon, will you need men to follow you?” Pilgrim said, “I need no men. I ask only that a few elderly and virtuous gentlemen sit quietly with my master and keep him company, so that I may leave him here and go. When I have caught that fiend and brought him here, we shall question him before everyone, and I will uproot the evil for you.” The old man immediately summoned a houseboy and had several relatives and friends invited. They all arrived before long, and after greetings had been exchanged, Pilgrim said, “Master, sit here at ease and do not worry. Old Monkey is off.”

p.src: She came forward, and upon seeing Old Gao, seized him, embraced him, and wept bitterly against his shoulder. Pilgrim said, “Do not cry yet, do not cry. Tell me, where has the monster gone?” The young woman replied, “I do not know where he goes. All this time, he has left at daybreak and returned only after nightfall. He comes and goes amid clouds and mist, and I do not know where he travels. Because he learned that Father wanted to drive him away, he has been constantly on his guard, and for that reason he comes at dusk and departs at dawn.” Pilgrim said, “Say no more. Old man, take your honored daughter to the front residence and speak at leisure of all that has happened during your separation. Let Old Monkey wait for him here. If he does not come, you must not blame me; but if he does come, I shall certainly uproot the evil for you.” Old Gao joyfully took his daughter away to the front residence.

p.src: When that fierce wind had passed, a monster appeared in midair, truly hideous in form: a black face covered in short hair, with a long snout and great ears; he wore a coarse robe of an uncertain greenish blue, with a figured cloth tied around his waist. The Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “So this is the fellow.” The fine Pilgrim neither went to meet him nor questioned him, but lay on the bed feigning illness and groaned and moaned without cease. Unable to tell true from false, the monster entered the room, clasped him in his arms, and tried to kiss him. The Pilgrim laughed to himself. “He really means to make sport with old Sun!” At once he used a grappling trick, propping up the monster’s long snout and executing what was called a little throw. With a toss of his head, he sent him crashing off the bed. The monster scrambled up, leaned against the bedside, and said, “Sister, why are you somewhat displeased with me today? Could it be because I came late?” “I am not displeased, not displeased,” said the Pilgrim. The monster said, “If you are not displeased with me, why did you throw me down like that?” The Pilgrim said, “Why are you so lacking in delicacy, embracing and kissing me the moment you arrive? I am feeling a little unwell today; had I been as well as usual, I would have risen and opened the door to await you. Take off your clothes and go to sleep.” The monster failed to grasp his meaning and actually went to undress. The Pilgrim leaped up and sat on the chamber pot. The monster returned to the bed as before and felt about, but finding no one there, called, “Sister, where have you gone? Please take off your clothes and come to bed.” The Pilgrim said, “You go to sleep first. Wait until I have relieved myself.” The monster duly undressed first and climbed into bed.

p.src: Suddenly the Pilgrim sighed and said, “My fortune has declined.” The monster said, “What are you fretting about? How has your fortune declined? Since I came to your household, though I have eaten some of your food and drunk some of your tea, I have never consumed them for nothing. I have swept your grounds and cleared your ditches, carried bricks and transported tiles, rammed earth and built walls, ploughed fields and harrowed soil, sown wheat and planted rice, and founded a thriving estate for your family. Now you wear brocade and adorn yourself with gold; in every season you enjoy flowers and fruit, and at every festival vegetables are cooked for you. What can still be unsatisfactory that you sigh so mournfully and speak of your fortune declining?” The Pilgrim said, “That is not what I mean. Today my parents, from beyond the wall, hurled bricks and tiles at me and reviled me bitterly.” The monster said, “Why did they beat and revile you?” The Pilgrim said, “They said that since you and I have become husband and wife and you are their son-in-law, you have shown no proper courtesy at all. A man with such an ugly face neither pays respects to his wife’s kin nor meets her relatives. Nor do they know, with all your coming on clouds and departing in mist, what family you truly come from, what your surname is, or what your name may be. You have tarnished their good repute and disgraced their family tradition. That is why they beat and revile me so, and why I am troubled.” The monster said, “Though I am somewhat ugly, it would not be difficult for me to become handsome if that were wanted. When I first came, I spoke with him about all this, and he agreed before taking me as his son-in-law. Why does he raise the matter again today? My home is in Cloud Path Cave on Mount Fuling. I took my surname from my appearance and am therefore surnamed Zhu; my formal name is Zhu Ganglie. If he questions you again, simply tell him this.”

p.src: The Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “This monster is remarkably honest. Without any torture, he has confessed everything so clearly. Now that I have his dwelling place and name, I shall capture him no matter what.” The Pilgrim said, “He means to invite a master of magic to capture you.” The monster laughed. “Sleep, sleep, and pay him no heed. I possess the thirty-six transformations of the Heavenly Stems and a nine-pronged muckrake. Why should I fear any master of magic, Buddhist monk, or Daoist priest? Even if your father were devout enough to summon the Great Patriarch Demon-Queller of the Ninth Heaven down to earth, I have known him before, and even he would not dare do anything to me.” The Pilgrim said, “He says he will invite Sun Wukong, the Great Sage Equaling Heaven who caused havoc in the Celestial Palace five hundred years ago, to come and capture you.” On hearing this name, the monster grew somewhat afraid and said, “If that is so, I had better leave. We cannot remain husband and wife.” The Pilgrim said, “Why leave so suddenly?” The monster said, “You do not understand. That Protector of Horses who caused havoc in Heaven has considerable ability. I fear I may be no match for him; then my reputation would suffer, and I would cut a sorry figure.”

p.src: With that, he put on his clothes, opened the door, and started outside. The Pilgrim seized him with one hand, wiped his own face, revealed his true form, and shouted, “You vile monster, where do you think you are going? Raise your head and see who I am!” The monster turned his eyes and saw the Pilgrim baring his teeth and twisting his mouth, with fiery golden eyes and a hairy, angular face, looking just like a living Thunder God. His hands went numb and his legs grew weak with fright. With a ripping sound he tore free of his clothes, transformed into a raging wind, and escaped. The Pilgrim rushed forward, drew his iron staff, and struck once at the wind. The monster transformed into myriad streaks of fire and sped straight back toward his mountain. The Pilgrim mounted a cloud and pursued him, crying, “Where do you think you are going? If you ascend to Heaven, I shall chase you to the Palace of the Dipper and the Ox; if you enter the earth, I shall pursue you to the Hell of the Wrongfully Dead!”
